lesson.title: A Labor Crisis Answered with a New Atlantic Trade
lesson.summary: As indigenous labor systems like the encomienda collapsed under disease and abuse, Spanish and Portuguese colonizers turned to enslaved Africans to work American mines and plantations, beginning a trade that would eventually transport millions across the Atlantic.
lesson.body:
Portugal, not Spain, pioneered the trade that would eventually reshape the Americas. Beginning in the mid-1400s under the sponsorship of Portuguese nobility, Portuguese ships worked their way down the West African coast, initially trading for gold and pepper and establishing fortified trading posts such as Elmina, built on the Gold Coast in 1482. Slavery already existed within many African societies and in the wider Mediterranean and Islamic world, and Portuguese traders inserted themselves into these existing networks, purchasing captive people from African merchants and rulers and shipping small numbers to Europe well before Columbus ever reached the Americas.

The scale and purpose of the trade changed once Spain's American colonies revealed a labor problem the encomienda system could not solve. Indigenous populations, already forced into brutal labor under encomenderos, were dying from European diseases at a pace that made them an unreliable and rapidly shrinking workforce. Sugar cultivation, in particular, demanded intense, sustained labor on plantations, and colonists looked across the Atlantic to the source Portugal had already developed.

Bartolome de las Casas, the Dominican friar who fought so hard against indigenous forced labor, plays an uncomfortable role in this history. Early in his career he suggested that enslaved Africans might replace indigenous workers in the hardest colonial labor, a position he later regretted and explicitly renounced as he came to see African enslavement as equally unjust. His shifting stance reflects how deeply the labor demands of colonization pushed Spanish colonial society toward viewing African slavery as an acceptable solution, regardless of individual moral objections.

The first enslaved Africans arrived in Spanish Caribbean colonies in the early 1500s, and the trade expanded steadily over the following century, tied closely to the growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean and, after 1500, in Portuguese Brazil. Ships typically carried European manufactured goods to West African coastal trading posts, exchanged them for captives, transported those captives across the Atlantic in the horrific conditions of the Middle Passage, and carried American sugar, silver, and other goods back to Europe, a circuit that later generations would call the Atlantic or triangular trade.

English colonization arrived on the scene generations after this system was already established. The first documented Africans in English North America arrived at Jamestown in August 1619, brought aboard a ship after being seized from a Portuguese slave vessel bound for the Spanish colonies. Their arrival did not immediately create the racialized, hereditary slave system that would later define the Chesapeake and the South; that would develop gradually over the following decades. But it placed English Virginia within a trans-Atlantic system of forced African labor that Spain and Portugal had built more than a century earlier, out of the same colonial labor pressures that had already transformed the encomienda system into something even darker.
